Get started with zurand

Source: vignettes/zurand.Rmd
zurand.Rmd
library(zurand)

R’s own generator keeps a hidden state. set.seed() fixes where it starts, and every call to runif() or rnorm() moves it on, so each number depends on everything drawn before it. zurand has no such state. In this vignette we bootstrap the mean of a small sample, and along the way meet keys, the samplers, key vectors and folding. Why the values are the same on every machine, and how fast they are, is left to the articles.

Make a key

A key is an immutable value made from a seed. Every random value is a pure function of a key and the value’s position, so the same key always gives the same numbers:

key <- rng_key(2026)
key
#> <rng_key> rng_key[91948d23db9c5598ed35455d78bc927d]
rng_uniform(key, 3)
#> [1] 0.15037421 0.91830293 0.06342998
rng_uniform(key, 3)
#> [1] 0.15037421 0.91830293 0.06342998

Asking for more values extends the sequence rather than changing it. The first three of six are the three above:

rng_uniform(key, 6)
#> [1] 0.15037421 0.91830293 0.06342998 0.74915105 0.60528900 0.30633444

Drawing uses nothing up: the key is the same afterwards, so there is no state to pass between functions, save or restore.

Draw from a key

The samplers are rng_uniform(), rng_normal(), rng_integer() and rng_bits(). Each takes a key and a count, then the parameters of its distribution. Here is the sample we will bootstrap, and one resample of it, drawn as positions between 1 and 8:

x <- c(2.1, 3.4, 1.9, 5.6, 4.2, 3.3, 2.8, 4.9)
i <- rng_integer(key, length(x), min = 1, max = length(x))
i
#> [1] 3 7 2 7 2 8 5 2
mean(x[i])
#> [1] 3.35

rng_normal() takes mean and sd, and rng_uniform() takes min and max, in the same way.

One key per replicate

A bootstrap needs many resamples, each from its own stream. rng_key() makes a key vector when asked for n keys, and a sampler given a key vector returns a matrix with one column per key:

keys <- rng_key(2026, n = 200)
length(keys)
#> [1] 200
idx <- rng_integer(keys, length(x), min = 1, max = length(x))
dim(idx)
#> [1]   8 200

Each column is one resample, so the bootstrap distribution of the mean is one line away:

boot <- apply(idx, 2, function(i) mean(x[i]))
quantile(boot, c(0.025, 0.975))
#>     2.5%    97.5% 
#> 2.799062 4.451250

A key vector can be indexed like any vector. Replicate 7 alone gives the same resample as column 7 of the matrix, so a replicate can be rerun without the others:

identical(rng_integer(keys[7], length(x), min = 1, max = length(x)), idx[, 7])
#> [1] TRUE

Name the parts with folding

Counting keys works while a computation has one part. When it has several, derive each part’s key from what the part is. rng_fold() takes a key and some data, a name or a number, and returns a new key; the same data always gives the same key:

boot_key <- rng_fold(key, "bootstrap")
replicate_key <- function(b) rng_fold(boot_key, b)
rng_uniform(replicate_key(3), 2)
#> [1] 0.3819716 0.5885736
rng_uniform(replicate_key(3), 2)
#> [1] 0.3819716 0.5885736

Because replicate b gets its numbers from its own key, the bootstrap gives the same answer whatever order the replicates run in. Here they run once in order and once shuffled, as parallel workers might run them (sample() only picks the order):

boot_mean <- function(b) {
  i <- rng_integer(replicate_key(b), length(x), min = 1, max = length(x))
  mean(x[i])
}
in_order <- vapply(1:200, boot_mean, numeric(1))

shuffled <- numeric(200)
run_order <- sample(200)
shuffled[run_order] <- vapply(run_order, boot_mean, numeric(1))
identical(in_order, shuffled)
#> [1] TRUE

A new part of the analysis, folded under another name, cannot change these values. The same holds for zurand’s own threads: rng_threads() changes how fast a large draw is made, never what it contains.

Vectors of any length

rng_lazy_normal() and rng_lazy_uniform() return a lazy vector: it holds only its key and arguments, and computes a value when it is read. A billion values are created at once, and they are the values the ordinary sampler gives:

z <- rng_lazy_normal(key, 1e9)
length(z)
#> [1] 1000000000
z[1:3]
#> [1]  0.006686381 -1.233412249  0.591067060
rng_normal(key, 3)
#> [1]  0.006686381 -1.233412249  0.591067060

A common mistake

The samplers take a key, not a seed. Passing the seed itself is an error that says what to do instead:

rng_normal(2026, 3)
#> Error in `rng_normal()`:
#> ! `key` must be an <rng_key>; create one with rng_key()
